questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify external political efficacy in a description
questions.stem: Memo from the planning office, Kestrel Row: the memo says residents assume their council will act on the evidence they send, and most feel able to see results. Which idea does the memo describe?

options.text: External political efficacy, the belief that government responds to people like us
Internal political efficacy, the belief that people like us can make a difference
options.misconception: confuses responsiveness of officials with citizens' own influence

options.text: Political indifference, shown by assuming that nothing sent is ever read
options.misconception: reads confidence in the council as political apathy

options.text: Diffuse political support, shown by agreeing with the council's general aims
options.misconception: confuses agreement with policy and a sense of influence

questions.explanation: External efficacy is the belief that officials respond to those who make demands, matching the memo. Internal efficacy concerns our own influence, and agreeing with policy is not efficacy.
questions.hint: Ask whether officials or citizens are expected to act.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data on party identification
questions.stem: File note, Harbour Road: the note records that 58 percent of voters say they feel closer to one party than to any other, while 22 percent feel equally close to several. What does this show?

options.text: Most voters float between parties without any stable preference at all
options.misconception: treats a 22 percent group as if it described all voters

options.text: Most voters report a stable party tie, with a sizeable floating group alongside
Voters are evenly split between those with and without a party tie
options.misconception: assumes the two figures must sum to a balance

options.text: The figures show that party identification has no measurable effect here
options.misconception: declines a conclusion the data does not support

questions.explanation: A 58 percent majority report feeling closer to one party, so identification is the norm, with 22 percent floating alongside it. The two groups need not balance, and the figures say nothing about effects.
questions.hint: Compare the 58 percent figure with the 22 percent figure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the free-rider problem in a collective campaign
questions.stem: Briefing slip, Vestry Yard: the slip notes a residents' group that will not pay for a legal challenge because the neighbours will, and every member reasons the same way. Why does the group raise nothing?

answer.exemplar: Each member expects the others to fund the challenge, so each waits for the others to act and no one contributes. The campaign is a collective good: once it exists everyone benefits whether or not they paid, so every individual has an incentive to free ride, which is why the group fails to raise the money it needs.

questions.explanation: The benefit is collective while the cost is individual, so each member waits for others to pay. That is the free-rider problem, and it stops a group that would benefit from acting together.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits once the challenge is funded.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate usable ballots lost to administrative failure
questions.stem: Case note, Copper Street: in a ward of 5,000 registered electors, 1,250 postal votes were applied for, but 310 of the ballots were returned as undeliverable. How many usable postal votes were cast?
questions.explanation: Of the 1,250 ballots applied for, 310 never reached the voter, leaving 940 usable postal votes. The undeliverable ballots are an administrative failure rather than a decision by any voter.
questions.hint: Subtract the undeliverable ballots from those applied for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the requirements of an initiative referendum

stimulus.body: The notice explains that residents may place a proposal on the ballot by collecting signatures equal to 5 percent of the registered electorate. The council must check the signatures and then hold a referendum, and a proposal on the ballot is decided by a simple majority of votes cast. Signatures that do not meet the published rules are returned and do not count.

questions.stem: Case note, Copper Street: the note below sets out the proposal route. Under this scheme, what is required for a proposal to reach the ballot?

options.text: A majority of the council's members must vote for the proposal beforehand
options.misconception: assumes the council must approve the proposal before the vote

options.text: The signatures of a majority of the electorate, verified by the council
options.misconception: inflates the signature threshold from a share to a majority

options.text: A signature threshold met and checked, followed by a referendum decided by a majority
A hearing before the council, after which the council publishes the question
options.misconception: mistakes a council hearing for a referendum ballot

questions.explanation: The route needs a signature threshold met and checked, then a referendum decided by majority. The council does not approve the proposal, and the threshold is a share of electors, not a majority.
questions.hint: Check what comes before the ballot and who validates it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a consumer boycott in a description
questions.stem: Planning memo, Ellersby: the memo says residents will stop buying from the firm whose lorry blocks the square, until the firm changes its routes. Which idea does the memo describe?

options.text: Vote buying, where consumers exchange money for a political favour
options.misconception: confuses refusing to buy with paying for influence

options.text: Ballot recycling, where a campaign reuses the same voters repeatedly
options.misconception: invents a voting practice the memo never mentions

options.text: Institutionalised protest, where a decision is taken by a permanent body
options.misconception: reads collective action as a decision by an institution

options.text: Consumer boycott, where buying is withdrawn to change a firm's behaviour

questions.explanation: A boycott works by withdrawing purchases to change a seller's behaviour, which is the memo's plan. Refusing to buy is not paying for influence, and collective consumer action is not a decision by an institution.
questions.hint: Ask what the residents stop doing and why.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a turnout gradient by deprivation
questions.stem: Note to committee, Sable Wharf: the note compares turnout of 74 percent in the least deprived ward and 41 percent in the most deprived ward. What does this pattern show?

options.text: Turnout falls as deprivation rises, forming a gradient across the city
Turnout rises as deprivation rises, because poorer areas are mobilised more
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the relationship

options.text: Deprivation has no bearing on turnout, since the wards differ in other ways
options.misconception: denies a relationship without examining the figures

options.text: Turnout is higher in deprived areas, but only for local elections
options.misconception: adds a claim about election type the note omits

questions.explanation: Turnout of 74 percent in the least deprived ward against 41 percent in the most deprived shows turnout falling as deprivation rises. Two wards cannot prove causation, but the gradient is visible.
questions.hint: Compare the two ends of the deprivation scale.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how media coverage sets the agenda
questions.stem: Site file, Marlow Rise: the file shows a coverage dispute that ran for two weeks because a newsletter asked about it, while nothing happened for a year before that. How did the question become an issue?

answer.exemplar: The media coverage set the agenda by raising a matter that nobody had placed on the council's list of business. Agenda setting is the power to determine which problems are treated as requiring a decision at all, and once a subject occupies the public agenda other actors, officials included, must respond to it and can no longer treat it as something nobody has raised.

questions.explanation: The newsletter did not decide the dispute, but it made it a question officials had to answer. Agenda setting is about which matters are treated as needing a decision at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the newsletter changed before any decision was made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of strategic voters in a survey
questions.stem: Memo, Quarry Lane: a poll of 30,000 voters found 18,000 would vote for their first preference, while 9,000 of those said they would switch to the candidate most likely to win if their first choice was behind. How many were making a strategic choice?
questions.explanation: The 9,000 who said they would switch to a candidate who could win are the strategic voters, and they are a subset of the 18,000 first preference voters. The remaining 21,000 of the poll were not voting at all.
questions.hint: Read the strategic group from the first preference group.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe a cleavage structure from survey shares

stimulus.body: The survey records that 41 percent of voters place themselves in the main working class party, 33 percent in the main middle class party, 14 percent support a regional party based on territory, and 12 percent support none of these. The report notes that class and territory lines cross in the same households, and that the divisions overlap rather than replace one another.

questions.stem: Report card, Dockside: the survey below describes party support. Which description of the structure is correct?

options.text: A single dominant cleavage with a small floating group attached to it
options.misconception: ignores the territorial party and the cross-cutting patterns

options.text: Two main class lines with a territorial party cutting across them
A territorial cleavage that has displaced both of the class alignments
options.misconception: treats a 14 percent party as having replaced the class lines

options.text: No stable structure, since the report says the lines cross within households
options.misconception: reads overlapping patterns as an absence of structure

questions.explanation: Class lines of 41 and 33 percent are the main divisions, and a territorial party of 14 percent cuts across them. The report's note that lines cross within households describes overlap, not the absence of structure.
questions.hint: Look at which party is the territorial one and how large it is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of weak external efficacy
questions.stem: Working note, Ashcroft: the note says people here vote, read the paper, and then nothing appears to change, so the effort seems pointless. What does that judgement rest on?

answer.exemplar: The judgement rests on a belief that the political system does not respond to people like the writer, which is external political efficacy. The gap between ordinary activity such as voting and the absence of visible results is what makes the effort look futile, and where such a belief is widely held, ordinary political action tends to fall away because its expected reward is close to zero.

questions.explanation: The note describes a belief that the system does not respond to ordinary people, which is external inefficacy. Where that belief spreads, routine political effort tends to stop because no return is expected.
questions.hint: Name the belief about how the system responds to ordinary people.

questions.explanation: The 520 identifying voters out of 800 surveyed is 0.65, that is 65 percent. The remaining 280 are distributed among floating voters and non-voters rather than forming a single alternative group.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the free-rider problem in a fundraising case

stimulus.body: The notice states that the residents' association must raise 4,000 to fund a legal challenge, that members are asked to contribute what they can, and that the challenge benefits every resident whether or not they pay. Last year's drive raised 900 in total, and the chair notes that a handful of members provided most of it.

questions.stem: Officer note, Tanfield Basin: the notice below describes the appeal. What does it illustrate?

options.text: A successful collective action, since the challenge went ahead despite the weak response
options.misconception: treats the appeal existing as proof the problem was solved

options.text: A leadership failure, since the chair should have appointed a treasurer
options.misconception: reduces the shortfall to a matter of internal appointments

options.text: A free-rider problem, since many benefit but few are willing to pay
A legality problem, since voluntary contributions cannot fund legal action
options.misconception: invents a legal obstacle the notice does not raise

questions.explanation: The challenge benefits every resident while the cost falls on those who pay, so most members wait and the total is far short of the target. That mismatch is the free-rider problem, not a failure of leadership.
questions.hint: Ask who receives the benefit and who bears the cost.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an administrative barrier to voting
questions.stem: Site memo, Havelock Row: the memo says many residents cannot register at the hall because it opens only during working hours, and the online route needs a photo identity document. What is at issue?

options.text: A psychological barrier, because residents lose interest in politics
options.misconception: treats inconvenient opening hours as a loss of interest

options.text: A socioeconomic barrier, because poorer households vote less often
options.misconception: confuses an administrative obstacle with income differences

options.text: A legal barrier, because the registration law itself deters applications
options.misconception: assumes the law prohibits evening registration

options.text: An administrative barrier, because the rules for registering are hard to satisfy

questions.explanation: Opening hours and documentary requirements are rules for registering that residents cannot easily meet, so they are administrative barriers. Interest, income and the legality of the rules are not what the memo describes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the obstacle lies in the paperwork or in attitudes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Trace the stages of an initiative referendum
questions.stem: File note, Princes Gate: the note records that 1,520 signatures were submitted for the proposal, 1,140 were verified as valid, and the proposal then went to a poll which the measure won by 61 percent. What does the sequence show?

options.text: A verified signature threshold, followed by a direct vote, with the measure carried
A council vote that rejected the proposal before any poll was held
options.misconception: invents a council stage the sequence does not contain

options.text: A poll that failed because too few of the signatures were valid
options.misconception: reads the 75 percent of valid signatures as a shortfall

options.text: A campaign that succeeded without meeting any signature requirement
options.misconception: ignores the requirement that the notice actually sets

questions.explanation: Signatures were collected and checked, then the question went to a direct poll the measure won by 61 percent, so the threshold was met and voters decided. No council stage appears in the sequence.
questions.hint: Follow the steps in the order the note lists them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conditions a boycott requires
questions.stem: Globe-side notes, Marden Wharf: the writer notes that the shop was the only one in town, so residents kept buying while complaining, and nothing changed. Why did the pressure fail?

answer.exemplar: A boycott only bites when a significant share of customers can withdraw their custom and can move it elsewhere. With a single supplier, refusing to buy mainly punishes the boycotters themselves, and moving demand to a competitor is impossible because no competitor exists, so the threat of withdrawal is not credible and the firm's behaviour does not change.

questions.explanation: A boycott needs somewhere else to buy and enough people willing to go, and with one shop both conditions fail. Complaints without a credible alternative leave the firm's behaviour unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask whether refusing to buy has anywhere else to go.

questions.learningObjective: Compare turnout counts across two wards
questions.stem: Minute, Gallowgate: turnout was 62 percent in a ward of 8,000 registered electors and 78 percent in a ward of 5,000 registered electors. How many more ballots were cast in the first ward?
questions.explanation: The first ward cast 4,960 ballots and the second cast 3,900, so the first ward recorded 1,060 more ballots. The second ward's higher rate did not overcome its much smaller electorate.
questions.hint: Work out the ballots cast in each ward, then subtract.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how agenda rules exclude a public issue

stimulus.body: The letter states that the committee will not consider the proposal in this session because the business list is already fixed, and that the chair offers to raise the matter as a point of order. A separate note records that the issue received more than 300 letters and a television slot, yet the matter was never scheduled for debate.

questions.stem: Memorandum, Wharf Crescent: the letter and note below concern a matter that was widely raised. What do they show?

options.text: The issue failed because there were too few letters to reach the threshold
options.misconception: treats the volume of publicity as the cause of exclusion

options.text: The agenda-setting gate kept the matter out even though the public raised it
The issue was excluded because the television coverage was hostile to the firm
options.misconception: invents a motive for exclusion the papers do not state

options.text: The issue was excluded because the proposal was legally defective
options.misconception: adds a legal defect that no document in the file mentions

questions.explanation: The business list was fixed and the matter never scheduled, so the agenda gate excluded it despite 300 letters and a television slot. Public pressure shapes the agenda only where procedure allows.
questions.hint: Ask what the council's own procedure did with the letters.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify strategic voting from a recorded preference
questions.stem: Minute, Wharf Crescent: the minute records that many supporters of a third party backed the leading candidate in second preferences, saying they did not want the third party to win and divide the vote. Which practice is described?

options.text: Party identification, since the voters are loyal to a single party throughout
options.misconception: treats a tactical switch as continuing loyalty

options.text: Free riding, since the voters benefit without adding their own support
options.misconception: confuses voting for a candidate with enjoying a public good

options.text: Strategic voting, since the vote is cast for a chance of winning
Turnout bias, since only committed supporters bothered to vote
options.misconception: reads a preference order as a decision not to vote

questions.explanation: Backing a candidate one would not otherwise prefer in order to stop another winning is strategic voting, judging which option can win. Continued loyalty is party identification, and ordering preferences is not about turnout.
questions.hint: Ask what the voters expected their vote to achieve.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret turnout differences by housing tenure
questions.stem: Planning note, Cordite Street: the note reports that turnout in postcodes where three quarters of homes are owner occupied is 71 percent, and 46 percent where only a quarter are owner occupied. What does this suggest?

options.text: Turnout is unrelated to housing tenure, since the two figures are close together
options.misconception: ignores the 25 point gap between the two figures

options.text: Owner occupation raises turnout, but only in the most deprived areas
options.misconception: adds a condition the note does not mention

options.text: Housing tenure has no effect on turnout once income is taken into account
options.misconception: claims a control that the note never applies

options.text: Turnout is higher where owner occupation is widespread, suggesting a tenure cleavage

questions.explanation: Turnout of 71 percent against 46 percent shows higher participation where owner occupation is common, consistent with a tenure cleavage. The note neither isolates income nor limits the effect to deprived areas.
questions.hint: Compare the two tenure groups directly.

questions.explanation: The 480 residents out of 1,200 surveyed is 0.40, that is 40 percent. The remaining 720 either did not feel heard or did not express a view at all.
questions.hint: Divide the respondents who felt heard by the total surveyed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the link between identification and turnout

stimulus.body: The note reports that in a ward of 6,000 electors, 4,350 turned out to vote, and of those who voted, 78 percent said they felt closer to one party than to any other. The note adds that the adjoining ward, where the same party has organised locally for thirty years, has a turnout of 66 percent and that only 41 percent of its voters report feeling close to a party.

questions.stem: Notice pinned in the hut, Yarwell: the note below reports turnout and identification. What does it support?

options.text: Turnout is higher where identification is stronger, which the two wards are consistent with
A causal claim that identification makes people vote, proved by comparing two wards
options.misconception: treats a difference between two wards as proof of cause

options.text: A finding that turnout is higher where fewer voters feel close to a party
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the reported relationship

options.text: A finding that organisational history has no effect on turnout at all
options.misconception: denies the difference the two figures display

questions.explanation: The ward with 78 percent identification turned out 72.5 percent against 66 percent where only 41 percent identify, consistent with identification supporting turnout. Two wards cannot establish causation, and the direction is not reversed.
questions.hint: Compare turnout and identification together in each ward.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify free riding in a shared service
questions.stem: Recollections written in 1998, Pentland: the writer recalls that a subscription service was cheaper when everyone in the building paid, and one family never paid because others did. What does the example show?

options.text: The problem of collective action, solved once enough people contribute to a service
options.misconception: describes a successful collective effort as a problem

options.text: The free-rider problem, since one member benefits without contributing
The problem of selective exposure, since the family avoided the service entirely
options.misconception: recalls the family's non-participation in a service

options.text: The problem of agenda setting, since the family set the price for everyone
options.misconception: misreads a subscription arrangement as control of the agenda

questions.explanation: The family enjoys the discount produced by its neighbours' payments while paying nothing, which is free riding on their contribution. A successful collective service is not itself a collective action problem.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from the discount and who created it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate requests that produced no usable vote
questions.stem: Working paper, Limehouse Rise: the paper reports that of 1,500 postal ballot requests, 380 were never sent out, 210 were sent to addresses that no longer existed, and 190 were returned unopened. How many requests produced no usable vote?

options.text: 190 requests, which is the number of unopened returns
options.misconception: counts only one of the three groups of failures

options.text: 380 requests, which is the number never dispatched
options.misconception: ignores the two later stages of failure

options.text: 780 requests, which is the sum of the three failure groups
590 requests, which excludes the unopened returns on purpose
options.misconception: leaves out one group without any stated reason

questions.explanation: Adding 380 undispatched, 210 wrongly addressed and 190 unopened gives 780 requests that produced no usable vote. Each group is a separate failure at a different stage, so none can be left out.
questions.hint: Add every group where the request failed to produce a ballot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the initiative route in the hands of organised campaigners
questions.stem: Site note, Brackley Reach: the note records that a petition on a local hospital attracted 9,000 signatures, most of them gathered by a single charity that already opposed the closure. What does the petition show about the initiative route?

answer.exemplar: The petition shows the vulnerability of the initiative route to organised mobilisation rather than to the weight of public opinion, because most of the 9,000 signatures came from one campaigning charity. Signature thresholds are easy for organised groups with existing networks to reach, so a successful initiative may reflect the resources of a campaign organisation rather than the distribution of opinion across the electorate.

questions.explanation: Signatures gathered mostly by one opposed organisation show how easily an initiative can be driven by organised campaigners, so reaching the threshold need not show that wider opinion favours the proposal.
questions.hint: Ask who gathered the signatures and with what resources.

questions.stem: Case summary, Dover Reach: a boycott removed 1,250 customers from a shop's weekly trade of 5,000, and 700 of those customers moved to a nearby competitor. How many customers were lost to the sector entirely?
questions.explanation: Of the 1,250 customers lost by the target shop, 700 moved to another firm, so 550 left the sector altogether. A boycott that simply shifts custom between rivals does not damage them all.
questions.hint: Subtract the customers who switched rivals from those who left.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a deprivation turnout gradient

stimulus.body: The paper records turnout of 38 percent in the most deprived ward, 55 percent in the middle band of wards, and 71 percent in the least deprived. It also notes that the most deprived ward has the highest proportion of people who say they have never voted and cannot name the local candidates, and that the pattern has persisted across three elections.

questions.stem: Brief, Halberd Street: the paper below reports turnout. What does it show?

options.text: Turnout is unrelated to deprivation, since the three wards are not directly comparable
options.misconception: dismisses a consistent pattern because the wards differ

options.text: Turnout is higher in deprived wards, because they have more local candidates to choose from
options.misconception: invents a candidate-supply explanation the paper does not give

options.text: Turnout is the same in every ward, with 38, 55 and 71 averaging to 55
options.misconception: treats three different figures as one averaged figure

options.text: A turnout gradient by deprivation, reinforced by the never-voted finding

questions.explanation: Turnout rises from 38 to 55 to 71 percent as deprivation falls, and the most deprived ward also has the most never-voted residents, reinforcing the pattern. A gradient is not itself a proven cause.
questions.hint: Look at the ordering of the three figures and the never-voted finding.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify agenda setting from an outcome
questions.stem: Record, Marden Wharf: the record shows that the tram replacement was debated for two hours after a petition and a newspaper story forced it onto the list, though the officers had rated it a low priority. Which idea is demonstrated?

options.text: Agenda setting, since external pressure moved the matter into the arena of decision
Executive dominance, since the officers' original low rating decided the outcome
options.misconception: suggests the officers determined the final decision

options.text: Diffuse review, since the matter was examined by many different participants
options.misconception: reads the length of a debate as wide participation

options.text: Cleavage structure, since the tram divided the town's two main class groups
options.misconception: asserts a class division the record never mentions

questions.explanation: The petition and press coverage decided what was discussed rather than what was decided, which is agenda setting. A debate's length says nothing about how many took part, and no class division is described.
questions.hint: Ask what the outside pressure changed: the topic or the outcome.

questions.stem: Internal note, Towpath Lane: the note records that in 40 three-way contests, the candidate leading on first preferences won 22 times, and 14 of the 22 wins came from voters whose first preference lay elsewhere. What does the note show?

options.misconception: confuses losing leaders with small party success

options.text: Voting is ideological, since most voters chose a candidate they already preferred
options.misconception: calls second preference voting ideological support

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a shift in the basis of political cleavage
questions.stem: Committee note, Verity Lane: the note describes a city where the main parties divide less by class and more by whether a household owns its home, and where a strong regional party draws its support from everywhere else. What is happening to the structure?

answer.exemplar: The structure is realigning around tenure rather than class, with a territorial party holding the remaining support, so the classic class cleavage has been replaced by a housing one. Such a shift changes which parties are viable, because the alignment of voters into groups now favours different organisations than the old class division did.

questions.explanation: The note describes a substitution of a tenure cleavage for a class one, with a regional party holding the rest, which is a change in the cleavage structure. It is not a claim that class has disappeared from politics.
questions.hint: Ask which line of division is doing the work now.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data on efficacy and contact

stimulus.body: The survey asked residents whether they thought their views on local services reached those who decide. Forty-one percent said they believed that they did, 33 percent said they were not sure, and 26 percent said they believed that they did not. A second question found that 58 percent of those who believed they were heard had contacted the council in the past year, compared with 19 percent of those who believed they were not.

questions.stem: Site file, Oysterman's Row: the survey below measures efficacy. What does it show?

options.text: Most residents believe they are ignored, since 26 percent say they are not heard
options.misconception: reads a minority group as a majority

options.text: Belief in being heard makes no difference to how often people make contact
options.misconception: denies the difference between the two contact rates

options.text: Belief in being heard is associated with a much greater rate of contacting the council
The survey shows that hearing residents causes 39 percent of them to vote
options.misconception: turns a contact rate into a voting effect

questions.explanation: Only 41 percent believe they are heard, and those who do are far more likely to have contacted the council, 58 against 19 percent, so efficacy and contact are strongly associated. The survey shows association, not causation.
questions.hint: Compare the contact rates of the two belief groups.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define party identification and its behavioural effects
questions.stem: Note, Cutter's Yard: the note says that people who think of themselves as supporters of a party are more likely to vote, to discuss politics and to keep up with the news. What does the note describe?

options.text: Political efficacy, because supporters feel their views are respected
options.misconception: confuses attachment to a party with a sense of influence

options.text: Turnout bias, because only committed supporters are counted as voters
options.misconception: treats a difference in participation as a counting practice

options.text: Resource mobilization, because supporters bring money and people to campaigns
options.misconception: reduces party attachment to the resources it supplies

options.text: Party identification, the sense of affinity with a party that shapes behaviour

questions.explanation: The note describes a felt affinity with a party that shapes political behaviour, which is party identification. Efficacy concerns being heard, and the note mentions no money, people or counting practices.
questions.hint: Ask what the supporters feel towards the party itself.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a burden-sharing failure
questions.stem: Planning slip, Cobbold Street: the slip records that 60 residents were asked to clean the canal path monthly, 9 volunteered, and the nine cleaners covered the whole year of work. What does the slip show?

options.text: A free-rider problem, since most residents left the burden to a small group
A successful collective action, since the work was completed as planned
options.misconception: ignores how few people carried the work

options.text: A turnout gradient, since volunteering rose with the size of the request
options.misconception: invents a link between request size and volunteering

options.text: A strategic voting case, since the nine chose the cheapest way to participate
options.misconception: reads volunteering for a task as a ballot decision

questions.explanation: Nine volunteers covered work that sixty residents had been asked to share, so the burden fell on a small group while others used the clean path for free. Completing the work does not make it a collective success.
questions.hint: Compare the number who were asked with the number who volunteered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain an administrative barrier arising from opening hours
questions.stem: Planning memo, Council House: the memo says the counting hall opens at eight in the morning, that people queue before dawn, and that many go home to work instead. What does the memo show?

answer.exemplar: The memo shows an administrative barrier: the rules for voting, in this case the hours of the count, are not designed around how people live. The cost of attending falls unevenly, so those with flexible working hours or private transport can comply while those without them cannot, which suppresses participation for reasons that have nothing to do with political opinion.

questions.explanation: Opening hours that clash with working life are a rule people cannot comply with, so turnout is reduced for reasons unrelated to opinion. The uneven cost of attending affects groups differently.
questions.hint: Ask what rule about voting some people cannot meet.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a signature threshold for a proposal
questions.stem: Working note, Sennick Row: a proposal must gather signatures equal to 5 percent of the 19,000 registered electors. How many signatures are required?
questions.explanation: Five percent of 19,000 electors is 0.05 times 19,000, which is 950 signatures. A figure of 3,800 would come from applying the share to the wrong base.
questions.hint: Take 5 percent of the number of registered electors.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge the success of a consumer boycott

stimulus.body: The report states that residents agreed not to buy petrol or fuel at the chain's stations until it reduced its deliveries to the estate, and that the campaign lasted eleven weeks. During the campaign the chain's sales to local households fell by 42 percent, while sales to households elsewhere in the area fell by 6 percent, and the company restored its earlier delivery schedule after the ninth week.

questions.stem: Case summary, Harrow Vale: the report below describes a boycott. What does it show?

options.text: The boycott failed, because the company changed its deliveries during the campaign
options.misconception: treats the outcome of a campaign as evidence it failed

options.text: The boycott worked, because the fall in local sales was far larger than elsewhere
The boycott worked only because competitors offered cheaper fuel nearby
options.misconception: credits price competition rather than the boycott

options.text: The fall in sales shows residents disliked the deliveries more than the price
options.misconception: infers a preference the report never records

questions.explanation: Local sales fell 42 percent against 6 percent elsewhere, so the boycott rather than a general trend best explains the fall, and the company altered its schedule during the campaign. The report mentions no cheaper competitor.
questions.hint: Compare the fall in local sales with the fall elsewhere.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Name the participation gradient by social advantage
questions.stem: Site memo, Fordington: the memo notes that turnout rises with income, with education and with home ownership, and that the group with the fewest of these characteristics votes least. What is the pattern called?

options.text: A turnout penalty, imposed deliberately on the least advantaged
options.misconception: assumes any uneven turnout must be designed policy

options.text: A mobilisation failure, caused by poor organisation in disadvantaged areas
options.misconception: treats a structural pattern as a campaign failing

options.text: A turnout gradient, in which participation rises with social advantage
A cleavage structure, describing the groups that vote differently
options.misconception: confuses the slope of turnout with divisions between groups

questions.explanation: A turnout gradient describes participation rising with income, education and home ownership, exactly as the memo lists. It is a pattern of unequal resources, not a deliberate penalty or an organisational failure.
questions.hint: Ask what the pattern describes about resources and voting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how issues reach the agenda
questions.stem: Site file, Harrow Vale: the file records 480 complaint letters, 35 press mentions and 12 items appearing on the council's public list of business. What does the file suggest about how issues reach the agenda?

options.text: Most issues reach the agenda by becoming complaint letters
options.misconception: assumes letters convert into agenda items one for one

options.text: Press coverage has the greatest effect, since 35 mentions produced most items
options.misconception: assumes the largest letter count produced the most items

options.text: The council's list is set by the number of complaints it receives each week
options.misconception: treats complaint volume as the only route onto the list

options.text: Public pressure matters, but the council's own procedures decide what is listed

questions.explanation: Only 12 of the 480 letters and 35 press mentions reached the list, so public pressure alone does not decide the agenda; the council's own business rules make the final selection.
questions.hint: Compare how many items were listed with how much pressure was applied.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate strategic voting as a rational response
questions.stem: Minute, Millward Row: the minute records that a survey found voters choosing the candidate they thought would win, and the writer asks whether this is dishonest. How should it be judged?

answer.exemplar: It is best judged as a rational response to a plurality system, because a voter who prefers a candidate who cannot win changes nothing by voting for them, while a vote for a possible winner can affect the result. Critics still argue that strategic voting hollows out the mandate, since the party that actually wins is not necessarily the one the voter most wanted.

questions.explanation: Strategic voting is a rational response to a plurality system, since a vote for a hopeless candidate changes nothing. Critics argue it hollows out the mandate, so the practice is defensible yet contested.
questions.hint: Ask what a vote for a candidate who cannot win can achieve.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the largest cleavage group as a share
questions.stem: Case file, Coldharbour Lane: a survey of 1,000 voters found 380 identify with the main working class party, 310 with the main middle class party, 150 with a regional party, and 160 with none of these. What percentage belong to the largest group?
questions.explanation: The largest group is the 380 identifying with the main working class party, and 380 out of 1,000 is 38 percent. The other two party groups are smaller, and those attached to none are a residual category rather than a cleavage.
questions.hint: Take the biggest group and divide by all 1,000 voters.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish external from internal political efficacy
questions.stem: Working note, Cormorant Yard: the note argues that the council is more likely to act when residents present a united front than when the same people make separate requests. Which idea is at work?

options.text: External political efficacy, since a united group is more likely to be answered
Internal political efficacy, since citizens feel able to make a difference themselves
options.misconception: confuses group influence with individual capacity

options.text: The pluralist model, where many groups compete for the government's attention
options.misconception: assumes a textbook label fits the situation

options.text: Collective action, where the cost of action is shared among many members
options.misconception: reads shared effort as the point rather than the response

questions.explanation: A united group that is answered shows responsiveness to demands, which is external efficacy. Internal efficacy is about one's own capacity, and the note's point is the response received, not the effort shared.
questions.hint: Ask whether the group's demands or its own capacity is at issue.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare party identification across voter groups
questions.stem: Memo, Valewood: the memo records that 62 percent of regular voters say they feel closer to one party, while only 29 percent of those who voted once say the same. What does the memo show?

options.text: Voting once is a sign of strong identification, because the rare voter is committed
options.misconception: inverts the pattern between voting and identification

options.text: Identification is stronger among regular voters, so it grows with political experience
Regular voters feel less attached to parties than occasional voters
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reported difference

options.text: Voting frequency is unrelated to any sense of party attachment
options.misconception: denies a relationship the two figures plainly show

questions.explanation: Regular voters report attachment at 62 percent against 29 percent for one-time voters, so identification grows with political experience. The reverse reading would need the opposite pattern in the figures.
questions.hint: Compare the 62 percent figure with the 29 percent figure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared benefit invites free riding
questions.stem: Brief, Dover Reach: the brief describes a scheme where each household is charged for its share of a new street light, and nine of twenty households pay nothing because the scheme works. Why is the scheme vulnerable?

answer.exemplar: Each household can be charged for what it uses, but the street light benefits every household whether or not it pays, so the unpaid households gain the same security as the paying ones. The contribution rule can be enforced on the nine who pay but not on those who opt out, and the result is a subsidy from the willing to the unwilling.

questions.explanation: The benefit is shared by all households while the cost falls on those who volunteer, so nine households free ride on the rest. The scheme transfers the cost of the light from the willing to the unwilling.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from the light and who is asked to pay.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate electors unable to cast a requested postal vote
questions.stem: Account book entry, Tanfield: in a ward of 12,000 registered electors, 4,800 applied for postal votes, 3,100 received ballots, and 2,400 returned completed ballots. How many electors who wanted a postal vote did not manage to cast one?
questions.explanation: Of the 4,800 who applied, only 2,400 returned a completed ballot, so 2,400 electors who wanted to vote by post did not manage to do so. The 700 ballots never received are part of that same shortfall.
questions.hint: Compare the number who applied with the number who voted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the outcome of an initiative poll

stimulus.body: The note records that a proposal to reopen the swimming pool was placed on the ballot after 1,100 signatures were verified, that the turnout at the poll was 38 percent against 61 percent at the previous election, and that the proposal was rejected by a margin of 340 votes. The note adds that a petition on the same question had been handed in twice before without reaching the signature threshold.

questions.stem: Memorandum, Cutter Street: the note below describes a proposal. What does it show?

options.text: The proposal failed because fewer people voted than at the previous election
options.misconception: blames the result on turnout rather than on votes cast

options.text: The petition route works poorly, since the second petition was rejected outright
options.misconception: describes a threshold failure as an outright rejection

options.text: The initiative route put the question to voters, who rejected it by 340 votes
The proposal failed because the council refused to schedule the poll
options.misconception: invents a refusal that the note contradicts

questions.explanation: The signatures were verified, the proposal went to the poll and it was rejected by 340 votes, so voters decided the question. Lower turnout is a different measurement, and the earlier petitions fell short of the threshold.
questions.hint: Follow the note: signatures, then poll, then margin.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a firm boycott from a market boycott
questions.stem: Report summary, Brackley Reach: the summary says residents stopped using the supermarket once its prices rose, but bought more at the discount store, so total local spending did not fall. Which idea is described?

options.text: Selective exposure, because residents chose only certain information about prices
options.misconception: describes information choice rather than spending choice

options.text: Consumer boycott, in which spending moves away from a firm without a market loss
A political protest, in which spending is withdrawn from the whole market
options.misconception: assumes a boycott must reduce spending across the sector

options.text: Agenda setting, because customers have forced the chain to change its prices
options.misconception: describes a price effect without evidence of any price change

questions.explanation: Spending shifted from one firm to another, which is a boycott of that firm even though the market as a whole keeps the money. Withdrawal from a whole market and any resulting price change are not shown here.
questions.hint: Ask which firm's sales fell and where the spending went.

questions.stem: Internal note, Sill Wharf: the note shows turnout of 31 percent among electors aged 18 to 24 and 72 percent among those aged 65 and over. What does the note show?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reported pattern

options.misconception: uses a difference in group size to dismiss the pattern

options.text: Turnout differences by age are a symptom of a single housing cleavage
options.misconception: reinterprets an age pattern as a housing effect

questions.explanation: Turnout of 31 percent for the youngest group against 72 percent for the oldest is a steep age gradient in participation. Group size does not explain it, and nothing in the note points to housing.
questions.hint: Compare the youngest and oldest groups directly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fixed agenda blocks a raised issue
questions.stem: Minute, Gower Reach: the minute records that the issue of park maintenance was raised at three separate meetings before the council agreed to discuss it, and the chair said the item was not on the list so could not be taken. What does the sequence show?

answer.exemplar: The sequence shows the difference between raising a matter and getting it decided. The chair could not take the issue because the agenda was already fixed, so the public had to keep the matter alive over three meetings before it was listed for discussion, which is the practical meaning of agenda setting as a gate on what gets debated at all.

questions.explanation: The chair could not take the matter because the list was fixed, so a fixed list is the gate on what gets debated. Persistent pressure eventually opened the gate, which is the practical shape of agenda setting.
questions.hint: Ask what stopped the matter being taken at the first meeting.

questions.stem: Memorandum, Quarrendon: a survey of 2,000 voters found 1,100 said they chose among the leading candidates, and 550 of those said they did so to avoid backing a candidate who might lose. What percentage of those 1,100 made a strategic choice?
questions.explanation: The 550 strategic voters out of 1,100 who chose among the leaders is 0.50, that is 50 percent. The other 550 of that group chose for other reasons, and the full survey included 900 who did not vote at all.
questions.hint: Divide the strategic group by the group of 1,100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret overlapping class and tenure cleavages

stimulus.body: The survey reports that 46 percent of voters identify with the main working class party, 29 percent with the main middle class party, 15 percent with a party defined by region, and 10 percent with none of these. It also reports that among voters who own their home, 58 percent identify with the middle class party, and among voters who rent, 71 percent identify with the working class party.

questions.stem: Planning file, Anchor Lane: the survey below describes party support. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The main divisions are regional, since 46 percent support the largest regional party
options.misconception: relabels the largest party as a regional party

options.text: Class and tenure reinforce each other, since owner occupation predicts middle class support
Party support is random, since the four percentages do not sum neatly to a pattern
options.misconception: treats a clear distribution as evidence of randomness

options.text: The regional party is a protest vote by renters, because 10 percent support nobody
options.misconception: invents a link between the regional party and renters

questions.explanation: The survey shows class and tenure overlapping: 58 percent of owners identify with the middle class party and 71 percent of renters with the working class party, so the two cleavages reinforce each other.
questions.hint: Look at how tenure predicts which class party is chosen.

The council acts on about a quarter of the concerns it receives
options.misconception: converts a perception figure into an action rate

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the durability of a turnout gradient
questions.stem: Bulletin, Havelock Green: the bulletin shows that turnout in the poorest fifth of the country is 41 percent and in the richest fifth is 73 percent, and it notes that the gap has narrowed only slightly in twenty years. What does the bulletin tell us?

answer.exemplar: The bulletin shows a steep and remarkably durable participation gradient, with a 32 point gap between the poorest and richest fifths that has barely narrowed in two decades. Persistent gaps of this kind point to structural causes such as differences in resources, work patterns and administrative ease of voting, rather than to short-lived campaigns or enthusiasm for a particular party.

questions.explanation: A 32 point gap that has barely narrowed in twenty years points to structural causes in resources, work patterns and voting arrangements rather than campaign enthusiasm. A persistent gap is not a permanent difference in interest.
questions.hint: Ask why a gap of this size has lasted so long.

questions.explanation: The weighted total is 1,200 from signatures, 1,200 from 600 press mentions at 2 each, and 200 from 40 motions at 5 each, giving 2,600. The score ranks the pressure on the issue, it does not decide the outcome.
questions.hint: Multiply each count by its weight, then add the three totals.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the decisive role of second preferences

stimulus.body: The briefing notes that the electoral system requires a candidate to reach 40 percent of the vote in the second round, and that in a poll of 25,000 voters 34 percent of first preference votes went to a candidate polling 12 percent, and 4 percent of voters gave that candidate a second preference. The briefing says the leading candidate reached 46 percent in the second round.

questions.stem: Committee report, Pendleton: the briefing below concerns how voters chose. What does it show?

options.text: The candidate polling 12 percent was the voters' second choice for most of the electorate
options.misconception: treats 4 percent of second preferences as a majority choice

options.text: The leading candidate's 46 percent came almost entirely from first preference votes
options.misconception: assumes second preferences were too few to matter

options.text: Second preferences determined the result, since the leading candidate needed 40 percent
Voting was entirely ideological, because the threshold was never in contention
options.misconception: ignores the threshold that made second preferences decisive

questions.explanation: The leader needed 40 percent and reached 46, and only 4 percent of voters gave a second preference to the 12 percent candidate, so second preferences were needed to clear the threshold.
questions.hint: Check the threshold against the leader's final share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe overlapping housing and age cleavages
questions.stem: Epitome, Thurlby: the epitome notes that the main parties now recruit almost entirely from homeowners, and that the main party of renters has a small but growing following among the young. What kind of structure does the epitome describe?

options.text: A class cleavage that has disappeared now that party labels dominate
options.misconception: claims the class line is gone because parties talk of other things

options.text: A single political cleavage cutting across all the other social divisions
options.misconception: reduces a two line structure to one undivided cleavage

options.text: No cleavage at all, since voters now choose on candidate image alone
options.misconception: denies the social pattern the epitome sets out

options.text: A tenure cleavage reinforced by age, with two housing and age lines overlapping

questions.explanation: Recruitment from homeowners plus growth among young renters describes a housing line crossed with an age line, so two overlapping cleavages structure the contest. Party labels dominate, but the social lines remain.
questions.hint: Ask which two social lines the epitome sets out.
